meta: Why has AI suddenly gotten so much better in the last few years? The secret is three sliders: push up the knobs, the data and the computing power (GPUs) together, and the error drops steadily.

muc.title: AI suddenly got much better
muc.text: Last time: a machine has to learn to understand, not memorize. So why has AI suddenly gotten so much better in the last few years? The secret: bigger.

muc.title: Three things get pushed up
muc.text: Picture three sliders. Slider one: the number of knobs in the network. Slider two: the amount of data to learn from. Slider three: computing power, meaning the number of graphics chips, called GPUs.

muc.title: Push them up, the error goes down
muc.text: People noticed that pushing all three up together makes the error drop quite steadily. These are called scaling laws. Thanks to them, people can roughly predict how much better a bigger model will be.

muc.title: Keep them balanced
muc.text: But they have to stay balanced. Lots of knobs with little data is like a big brain with just one book to read. Lots of data with few knobs is like a huge library with a tiny memory.

muc.title: Racing to build data centers
muc.text: That's why big companies race to build data centers with tens of thousands of chips, using a lot of electricity. It's also why big models are usually slower and pricier than small ones.

muc.title: Bigger isn't magic
muc.text: Getting one step better costs many times more, and the error only drops a little. So besides making models bigger, people also look for smarter ways to teach them.

muc.title: Small tasks, small models
muc.text: So you don't always need the biggest model. Translating a paragraph or summing up an email? A small model is fast and good enough. Video 18 shows how to choose.

muc.title: Does anyone understand the inside?
muc.text: With something that big, does anyone really understand what's going on inside? See you in part 7, the last part.
